epithet: Umm Ammarah — Shield of the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud
role: Warrior at the Battle of Uhud
Participant in the Second Pledge of Aqabah
One of the first women to pledge allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ
summary: Nusaybah bint Ka'b (RA), known as Umm Ammarah, was one of the most valiant women of the early Muslim community. She gave the second Pledge of Aqabah, nursed the wounded at Uhud, then took up sword and bow to defend the Prophet ﷺ directly when the battle turned against the Muslims — earning the Prophet's personal acknowledgment of her courage. She sustained twelve wounds at Uhud and went on to fight in subsequent campaigns.
biography:
Nusaybah bint Ka'b al-Ansariyyah al-Khazrajiyyah, known by her kunya Umm Ammarah, was a woman of the Banu Mazin clan within the Khazraj tribe of Madinah. She came from a family with a tradition of courage; her two sons Habib ibn Zayd and Abd Allah ibn Zayd were also Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and distinguished fighters.

Nusaybah was among the small group of Madinans — men and women — who traveled secretly to Makkah to give the Second Pledge of Aqabah in the twelfth year before the Hijrah (approximately 621 CE). Ibn Hisham records in al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah that seventy-three men and two women gave this pledge. Nusaybah was one of those two women, the other being Umm Mani' (Asma bint Amr al-Sulamiyyah). This pledge was the foundational covenant that invited the Prophet ﷺ to Madinah and established the basis for the Muslim community's safety there. Nusaybah's participation places her among the architects of the Hijrah itself.

Her most renowned moment came at the Battle of Uhud in 3 AH (625 CE). She had come to the battle carrying water and bandages, intending to nurse the wounded. But when the archers abandoned their position partway through the battle and the Quraysh cavalry encircled the Prophet ﷺ, Nusaybah put down her water skins, picked up a sword, and began fighting. She is described by al-Waqidi in Kitab al-Maghazi and by Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra as one of a small number of fighters who formed a close ring around the Prophet ﷺ to prevent his being killed.

The Prophet ﷺ observed her directly and was moved by what he saw. Nusaybah narrated herself: 'The Prophet ﷺ turned toward me — I was fighting on his right and his left — and he said: "Umm Ammarah, who can bear what you bear?"' She fought off multiple attackers and at one point engaged Ibn Qami'ah — the man who had badly wounded the Prophet ﷺ by striking his face — striking him with her sword repeatedly. She also used her bow. She received twelve wounds in the fighting, including a deep neck wound that took a year to heal. When the Prophet ﷺ saw her bleeding, he called to her son: 'Your mother! Your mother! Bind her wound, for your mother's station is higher than [that of many]!' (Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. 8)

After Uhud, Nusaybah's connection to the Prophet ﷺ deepened. She participated in the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (6 AH), the Conquest of Makkah (8 AH), the Battle of Hunayn (8 AH), and the Siege of Ta'if (8 AH). At Hunayn, when a portion of the army initially fled, she was among those who stood firm. She also participated in the expedition of Khaybar.

Perhaps the most painful test of her life was the fate of her son Habib ibn Zayd. During the apostasy (ridda) wars following the Prophet's death, Habib was captured by the false prophet Musaylimah al-Kadhdhab. Musaylimah asked him: 'Do you testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah?' Habib said yes. He then asked: 'Do you testify that I am the messenger of Allah?' Habib refused. Musaylimah cut him limb from limb, killing him piece by piece while he continued to affirm only the Prophet ﷺ. When Nusaybah heard, she swore to kill Musaylimah herself. She participated in the Battle of Yamama (12 AH / 633 CE) and fought with extraordinary ferocity. She lost her hand in that battle — her wrist was severed — but survived to see Musaylimah killed by Wahshi ibn Harb. Abu Bakr visited her afterward to honor her.

Nusaybah bint Ka'b died in Madinah around 13 AH (634 CE), during the caliphate of Abu Bakr. Al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' describes her as among the most courageous and distinguished women in the history of Islam. The Prophet ﷺ himself reportedly said: 'Whenever I turned to my right or left at Uhud, I saw Umm Ammarah fighting to protect me.' (Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra)

Emigrated with the Ansar community as the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah
Fought at the Battle of Uhud — defended the Prophet ﷺ directly; sustained twelve wounds including a deep neck wound
Participated in the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
Participated in the Conquest of Makkah, the Battle of Hunayn, and the Siege of Ta'if
Fought at the Battle of Yamama against Musaylimah to avenge her son Habib; lost her hand but survived

notable_traits: Direct personal defense of the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud — witnessed and praised by the Prophet himself
Sustained twelve wounds at Uhud including a near-fatal neck wound
Lost her hand at the Battle of Yamama — fighting to avenge her martyred son
One of only two women at the Second Pledge of Aqabah
